claim.text: BREAKING: Harwick council just slashed library funding by 40%. Eastgate and Millrow branches will close by spring. Shameful. #SaveHarwickLibraries

sources.title: City of Harwick - Regular Council Meeting Minutes (approved), Item 7: FY27 budget items
sources.text: 7a. Stormwater utility fee schedule. Staff presented the revised fee schedule for residential parcels. Councillor Pardo asked whether the senior discount would continue; staff confirmed it would. Received and filed. 7b. FY27 Draft Operating Budget. The Finance Director summarised the projected shortfall and the list of reductions proposed by departments. Motion (Obi / Chen) to reduce the Library Services line by 40 percent and to direct the City Manager to close the Eastgate and Millrow branches by 31 March. Discussion: Councillor Lindqvist said the motion 'guts a service people actually use'; Councillor Obi said the city 'cannot keep funding three buildings within a mile of each other'. Motion FAILED 3-6. Substitute motion (Lindqvist / Adeyemi) to reduce the Library Services line by 12 percent and direct staff to return with a study of options for the Eastgate and Millrow branches, including consolidation, shared use with the recreation department, or reduced hours. Substitute motion CARRIED 6-3. The Clerk noted that under Council Rule 14 any closure of a public facility requires a separate ordinance with two readings. 7c. Parking enforcement contract renewal. Deferred to the next meeting at the request of staff.

sources.headline: Council trims library budget after heated debate
sources.text: After nearly two hours of public comment, Harwick City Council on Tuesday approved a 12 percent reduction to library funding in the draft budget, rejecting a deeper 40 percent cut proposed by Councillor Obi. The approved motion asks staff to study the future of the Eastgate and Millrow branches, but no closures were voted on. 'A 12 percent cut will be felt - in hours, in staffing, in programs,' said Priya Nandakumar, president of the library workers' local. The budget returns for final adoption next month.

We have seen posts saying that Eastgate and Millrow will close. That is not correct. Council has asked staff to study options for those two branches and to report back. No branch is closing at this time, and all branches keep their current hours through the end of the fiscal year. We encourage residents to take part in the upcoming listening sessions.

HEADLINE: Coffee Reverses Aging, Scientists Confirm

SUBHEAD: Your morning cup could be the fountain of youth

BODY: Researchers at the Brannock Institute for Metabolic Research report that elderly mice given high doses of trigonelline, a compound found in roasted coffee beans, showed improved grip strength and longer running times compared with untreated mice over an eight-week study. The team also observed higher levels of a cellular energy molecule in muscle tissue. The study involved 24 mice and was published this week in a peer-reviewed journal. The authors caution that the dose used was far higher than anything a person could get from drinking coffee and that no human trials have been done. 'We would not suggest anyone change their coffee habits based on this,' said lead author Dr. Ines Farrow. 'This is an early step in understanding one pathway.' An independent researcher not involved in the study said the result was 'interesting but a long way from the clinic.'

claim.speaker: Rowan Tess, candidate for premier (fictional), speaking at a Northgate rally
claim.text: Under this government, unemployment in this province has doubled. Doubled! Ask anyone looking for work.
claim.video_context: The line came about twelve minutes into a forty-minute speech that also covered hospital wait lists, a promised ferry link and fuel taxes. The crowd of roughly three hundred, mostly local, cheered the line. Tess did not refer to young people or to any particular region in the minutes before or after it.

stat_release.text: Highlights. The provincial unemployment rate was essentially unchanged from the same quarter a year earlier. Employment grew in health care, construction and public administration and fell slightly in retail trade. The participation rate edged down, reflecting an ageing population. Youth unemployment (ages 15-24) rose over the year, driven mainly by fewer summer hires in accommodation and food services. Regional detail: the survey's regional breakdown groups the province into four economic regions; the Northgate area is included in the North economic region, for which the rate was also essentially unchanged. Long-term trend: the provincial rate remains lower than it was at the start of the current government's term. Technical note: estimates are subject to sampling variability; month-to-month changes in small regions should be interpreted with caution. Seasonally adjusted and unadjusted series are both available in the data tables. The next release is scheduled for the third quarter. Revisions: the first-quarter estimates were revised slightly upward following the annual benchmark to population estimates; the revision did not change the direction of any trend described above.

state.campaign_response: Asked about the figure, a Tess campaign spokesperson said the candidate 'was clearly talking about youth unemployment in Northgate, which everyone in that room is living with.' The spokesperson did not provide a source for a doubling.
state.reporter_note: We asked the statistics office for Northgate-only youth figures. The office said it does not publish youth unemployment below the economic-region level. We also asked the office whether any provincial series had doubled over the government's term; a spokesperson said none of the headline labour series had.
state.archive_note: Our desk rated a similar Tess claim last spring ('unemployment is up by half') as Mostly False after the campaign said it referred to a single town's plant closure. The campaign did not correct that claim on its website, and the line reappeared in two later speeches. Our standards editor asked that this check note the pattern but rate the new claim on its own evidence, as our guidelines require. A spokesperson for the governing party, contacted separately, called the doubling claim 'invented' and pointed to the long-term trend in the release; we do not rely on partisan statements for the rating.

article.headline: Marlowe Bay desalination plant clears final hurdle
article.body: The Marlowe Bay desalination plant cleared its last regulatory hurdle on Thursday when the regional water board approved its intake permit, ending a four-year review. The plant, which will cost $148 million to build, is designed to supply about a fifth of the peninsula's drinking water in dry years. Supporters on the water board said the plant would reduce the region's reliance on the Tanner Aquifer, which has dropped to record lows twice in the past decade. Opponents, including the Marlowe Bay Fishers' Cooperative, argued that the intake screens would harm larval fish and that the brine outflow had not been studied enough near the eelgrass beds. The permit requires the operator to fund an independent marine monitoring program for ten years and to cut intake flows during spawning season. Construction is expected to begin next spring. The operator, Peninsula Water Partners (fictional), said customer bills would rise by an amount it has not yet disclosed; the utility commission will review any rate change separately. Board member Liesel Okafor, who voted no, said she was 'not convinced the alternatives were taken seriously', pointing to a recycled-water proposal the board rejected last year. The cooperative's president, Arne Duval, said the group was reviewing its legal options but had not decided whether to challenge the permit. A spokesperson for the county said the plant's power supply would come partly from a solar array to be built on the former landfill site, which still needs its own planning approval. Local business groups welcomed the decision, citing the risk of water restrictions for restaurants and hotels during drought summers.
article.correction: Correction appended: An earlier version of this article misstated the construction cost of the plant. It is $148 million, not $480 million. The article has been updated.

preprint_record.title: Myocarditis signals after intranasal Vexlo administration in adolescents: a pharmacovigilance analysis
preprint_record.server_policy: Preprints are not peer reviewed. Withdrawn preprints remain visible with a notice; the original text is retained for the record.
preprint_record.abstract: Background: Vexlo is an intranasal decongestant licensed for ages 12 and over. We examined spontaneous adverse event reports mentioning Vexlo and myocarditis. Methods: We searched a national spontaneous reporting database for reports in adolescents aged 12 to 17 and calculated reporting odds ratios against all other nasal decongestants. Results: We identified reports suggesting a disproportionality signal. Limitations: spontaneous reports cannot establish incidence or causation; reporting may be stimulated by media coverage; duplicate reports are possible. Conclusions: Further study is warranted.
preprint_record.withdrawal_notice: The authors have withdrawn this manuscript. After posting, the authors identified a coding error that counted each follow-up report as a new case, inflating the number of cases approximately fifteen-fold. After correction, no disproportionality signal remains. The authors do not wish this work to be cited.

claim.text: Scientists agree: the new Callow Reservoir is causing the earthquakes around Dunfield. The government knew and filled it anyway.

sources.text: Since the Callow Reservoir began filling, the Survey's local network has recorded an increase in small earthquakes (all below magnitude 3) within 10 km of the dam. Reservoir-induced seismicity is a known phenomenon, and the Survey considers it a plausible contributor. However, the Dunfield area also experienced swarms of similar size in years before the reservoir existed, and the Survey's monitoring network was densified at the same time filling began, which increases the number of small events detected. The Survey is conducting a two-year study to separate these effects and has not reached a conclusion.

A team led by Dr. Anneke Visser (fictional) at Northfield University reports in a peer-reviewed paper that the timing and depth of recent events near Dunfield are 'strongly consistent with' reservoir loading. Visser said: 'I'm confident the reservoir is a major factor. Not every colleague agrees yet.'

Reservoir-induced seismicity is assessed as possible but of low probability, with any events expected to be minor. A monitoring network will be installed before filling. Filling will be slowed if events above magnitude 3.5 are recorded.

Residents say cracks have appeared in several older homes. The dam operator says no event has approached the magnitude 3.5 threshold. The county has offered free structural inspections, and an engineer who carried out several said most cracks she saw were consistent with settlement and seasonal ground movement, though she could not rule out vibration in two cases. A residents' group has asked for filling to be paused until the Survey's study is complete; the operator says the licence conditions do not require that.

sources.type: letter to the editor from a second seismologist
sources.text: Dr. Tomas Rehn (fictional), a seismologist at the Coastal Institute, wrote that the Visser paper 'does not adequately account for the denser network' and that the swarm pattern resembles pre-reservoir swarms in the 1990s. He said it was 'too early for anyone to claim a consensus in either direction'.

The dam operator's quarterly monitoring summary lists every event recorded by the network within 10 km of the dam, with magnitude, depth and time. The summary notes that the largest event this quarter was magnitude 2.6, that the reservoir is at 71 percent of its planned level, and that filling continues at the licensed rate. It states that the operator shares raw data with the Geological Survey weekly and will adjust filling immediately if the licence threshold is reached. An independent panel appointed under the licence reviews the summary each quarter; its last review found the monitoring adequate and recommended adding two more stations.

state.headline: Court Strikes Down City's Rent Cap
state.body: The state Court of Appeal on Friday struck down one provision of Ellisport's rent stabilisation ordinance, ruling that the city exceeded its authority when it applied the annual cap to single-family homes owned by individual landlords with two or fewer properties. The court left the rest of the ordinance in place, including the 4 percent annual cap on apartment buildings, which cover the large majority of the city's rental units. 'The cap stands for nearly every renter in Ellisport,' said city attorney Rosa Imbert. The landlords' association, which brought the case, called the ruling 'a partial victory' and said it was considering an appeal to the state Supreme Court on the remaining provisions. The ruling applied the ordinance's severability clause, which says that if any part is held invalid the remainder continues in effect. Tenant advocates said they would ask the council to explore other ways to protect renters in single-family homes. In a separate matter, the court declined to hear a challenge to the city's short-term rental registry.
state.ruling_excerpt: Section 5(c), to the extent it applies to single-family dwellings owned by natural persons holding no more than two rental properties, is invalid. Pursuant to Section 14 (severability), the remaining provisions of the ordinance are unaffected. The trial court's judgment is otherwise affirmed. Each party shall bear its own costs on appeal.
state.ordinance_s14: Section 14. Severability. If any provision of this ordinance or its application to any person or circumstance is held invalid, the invalidity does not affect other provisions or applications that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application.
social_reaction: Landlord forum: 'RENT CAP IS DEAD. Raise away.'
Tenant union: 'Read the ruling. Your cap still applies unless you rent a house from a small landlord.'

state.city_faq: Q: My apartment building has 12 units. Does the cap still apply? A: Yes. The ruling does not affect apartment buildings. Q: I rent a house from someone who owns only that house. A: The cap may no longer apply to you. Contact the rent board before accepting an increase above 4 percent; other protections, such as notice periods, still apply.
state.rent_board_note: The rent board said it had received more than two hundred calls since the ruling, most from apartment tenants whose landlords had cited the headline when proposing increases above the cap. The board reminded landlords that increases above 4 percent on covered apartments remain unlawful and can be challenged.

record.abstract: Background: Exercise is recommended for people with type 2 diabetes, but the effect of supervised combined aerobic and resistance training delivered in community gyms is uncertain. Methods: In this multicentre, parallel-group randomised controlled trial, we enrolled 212 adults aged 35 to 74 years with type 2 diabetes for at least one year and HbA1c between 7.0% and 10.0%. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) by a central web-based system to 16 weeks of supervised combined training three times per week or to usual care. Secondary outcomes included fasting plasma glucose, body weight, blood pressure and adverse events. Results: 198 participants (93%) completed the 16-week assessment. Four musculoskeletal adverse events occurred in the training group, none serious. Conclusions: Supervised combined training for 16 weeks improved glycaemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. Record REC-4410
Title: Proton pump inhibitor use and risk of community-acquired pneumonia in older adults: a population-based study

Abstract: Background: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are widely prescribed to older adults. Some studies suggest an association with pneumonia. Methods: Using a regional primary care database, we identified all adults aged 65 years and over with a first hospital admission for community-acquired pneumonia between two index years (cases). For each case, up to four controls without pneumonia were matched on age, sex, general practice and calendar time. Current PPI use was defined as a prescription within 30 days before the index date. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios adjusted for comorbidities and co-medications. Results: We included 6,112 cases and 23,904 matched controls. Current PPI use was associated with increased odds of pneumonia (adjusted OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.44). The association was strongest in the first 30 days after starting treatment. Conclusions: Current PPI use is associated with a modest increase in pneumonia risk in older adults; residual confounding cannot be excluded.

record.title: A randomised trial of a mindfulness app for anxiety in primary care
record.methods: Participants were recruited from 12 general practices. Adults aged 18 to 65 with a GAD-7 score of 8 or higher who owned a smartphone were eligible; people receiving psychological therapy were excluded. After baseline assessment, the research assistant opened the next envelope in a pile prepared by the trial statistician to reveal group allocation. Envelopes were not described as sealed or opaque. The allocation sequence was generated by computer in blocks of four. The intervention group received the Stillwater app (fictional) with eight weekly modules; the control group received a leaflet on anxiety and a list of local services. Participants and the research assistant who collected outcomes knew the allocation. The primary outcome was the GAD-7 score at 8 weeks, self-reported online. Secondary outcomes were PHQ-9 depression scores and app engagement (intervention group only).
record.results: Of 300 randomised participants, 186 completed the 8-week GAD-7 (intervention 81/150; control 105/150). Reasons for dropout were not reported. Analysis included completers only. GAD-7 scores were lower in the app group at 8 weeks. Median app engagement was three of eight modules.
record.registration: Registered retrospectively, after recruitment had finished.
record.funding: Funded by a university innovation grant. The app developer provided free licences and had no role in analysis, according to the authors.
record.discussion: The authors acknowledge that the completers-only analysis may overstate the effect if people who stopped using the app were those who did not benefit. They note that the leaflet control did not match the time and attention of the app, and that participants could not be blinded. They describe the trial as 'a pragmatic first evaluation' and call for a larger, prospectively registered trial with an attention-matched control and intention-to-treat analysis. No sensitivity analysis for missing data is reported, and the authors say the university's ethics committee did not require prospective registration at the time.

record.title: Monthly high-dose cholecalciferol and falls in older care-home residents: a double-blind randomised trial
record.abstract: Background: Falls are common among older people living in residential care, and vitamin D insufficiency is widespread in this group. Whether monthly high-dose supplementation reduces falls is uncertain. Methods: We randomised 684 residents aged 70 years or older from 41 care homes to 60,000 IU cholecalciferol or identical placebo capsules given monthly for 12 months. Residents with a history of kidney stones or hypercalcaemia were excluded. Care staff recorded falls prospectively in daily diaries using a standard definition; residents, care staff and investigators were blinded to allocation. The primary outcome was the rate of falls. Results: 642 residents (94%) completed follow-up. The rate of falls was 1.9 per person-year in the vitamin D group and 2.1 in the placebo group (rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.06). Fractures were infrequent in both groups. Hypercalcaemia occurred in three participants in the vitamin D group and one in the placebo group. Conclusions: Monthly high-dose vitamin D did not significantly reduce falls among care-home residents. Funding: Regional Health Research Fund (fictional); capsules supplied by the manufacturer, which had no role in the analysis.
record.discussion_excerpt: Our population differs from community-dwelling older adults in several ways. Care-home residents are frailer, more often cognitively impaired, and more likely to be vitamin D deficient at baseline; they also have more supervised mobility and different fall hazards. Earlier community trials used daily rather than monthly dosing. We therefore caution against extrapolating our null result to people living independently, while noting that the direction of effect was similar to that of recent community trials.

Record REC-2415
Title: Introducing a sepsis recognition bundle across hospital wards: a stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial

Abstract: Background: Delayed recognition of sepsis on general wards contributes to preventable deaths. Methods: Sixteen general medical and surgical wards in four hospitals were randomised to the order in which they crossed from usual care to a sepsis recognition bundle (electronic early-warning score with automated alerts, nurse education and a rapid-response escalation pathway). Every four months, four further wards crossed over, until all wards had the bundle. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality among patients with suspected sepsis; secondary outcomes were time to antibiotics and ICU admission. Analysis used mixed models adjusting for calendar time. Results: 9,412 patient episodes with suspected sepsis were included. Time to antibiotics was shorter under the bundle. In-hospital mortality was lower under the bundle, but the difference was not statistically significant after adjustment for time trends. Conclusions: The bundle shortened time to antibiotics; its effect on mortality is uncertain.

record.title: Acupressure wristbands for postoperative nausea after laparoscopic surgery: randomised sham-controlled trial
record.methods: Adults undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at two hospitals were randomised by a telephone service, using computer-generated blocks of variable size, to acupressure wristbands placed at the P6 point or to sham wristbands placed at a non-acupoint on the dorsal wrist. Bands were applied by theatre nurses in the anaesthetic room after induction. Patients were told they would receive 'one of two wristband positions being studied'. The primary outcome was patient-reported nausea severity on a 0-10 scale at 2, 6 and 24 hours after surgery, collected by ward nurses who were not told the allocation but could see the band position. Vomiting episodes and rescue antiemetic use were taken from the drug chart. All patients received standard antiemetic prophylaxis. Before discharge, patients were asked which band they thought they had received; 41% of the acupressure group and 38% of the sham group guessed 'real acupressure', and the rest guessed sham or did not know.
record.results: Of 260 randomised patients, 254 were analysed (intervention 127, sham 127); six were excluded after conversion to open surgery. Mean nausea scores were lower with acupressure at 6 hours (difference -0.9 points, 95% CI -1.6 to -0.2) but not at 2 or 24 hours. Rescue antiemetic use was similar between groups. No adverse events related to the bands were reported. Two patients in each group removed their bands early because of skin irritation; their data were retained in the analysis.
record.registration: Prospectively registered; the registry lists nausea at 6 hours as the primary time point, with 2 and 24 hours as secondary.
record.funding: No external funding. The wristband manufacturer supplied bands free of charge and had no other role.
record.discussion_excerpt: The benefit at 6 hours was modest and did not translate into reduced rescue antiemetic use. The blinding check suggests patients could not reliably tell which band they wore. We did not record whether ward nurses recognised the P6 position.

record.abstract: Methods: 1,860 patients within 30 days of myocardial infarction were randomised to colchicine 0.5 mg daily or placebo. Primary outcome: composite of cardiovascular death, recurrent myocardial infarction and stroke. Results: Median follow-up 22 months. The primary outcome occurred less often with colchicine (hazard ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.84). Diarrhoea was more frequent with colchicine. Conclusions: Colchicine reduced ischaemic events after myocardial infarction.

notices.text: The editors have been made aware of concerns about the integrity of data from three of the 41 sites in the COL-HEART trial. An investigation by the sponsoring institution is under way. Readers should interpret the findings with caution until the investigation concludes.

Following the conclusion of the institutional investigation, the article is retracted. The investigation found that data from three sites, contributing approximately 14 percent of randomised patients, had been fabricated. The remaining authors were unable to provide a reanalysis acceptable to the journal. All authors except the investigator responsible for the three sites agreed to the retraction.

record.institution_statement: The sponsoring university confirmed that the investigation concluded that one site investigator fabricated follow-up visits and outcome data for patients at three sites under his supervision. No evidence of misconduct was found at the other 38 sites. The investigator has left the university. The university has notified the national research integrity office and the trial registry, and has offered the remaining site-level data to independent groups on request, subject to ethics approval.

record.journal_statement: In a separate editorial, the journal explained that it considered publishing a corrected analysis limited to the 38 unaffected sites but decided against it because the trial's randomisation was stratified by site and the statistical analysis plan did not anticipate excluding sites; a post hoc subset would not carry the protections of the original design. record.title: Intensive versus standard glucose lowering after ischaemic stroke in type 2 diabetes: the GLU-STROKE randomised trial
record.abstract: Background: Hyperglycaemia is associated with poor outcomes after stroke, but the benefit of intensive glucose lowering in people with type 2 diabetes after ischaemic stroke is uncertain. Methods: In this open-label trial with blinded outcome adjudication, 1,410 adults with type 2 diabetes and ischaemic stroke in the previous three months were randomised to intensive (target HbA1c below 6.5%) or standard (target below 8.0%) glucose control. The primary outcome was recurrent stroke. Secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, severe hypoglycaemia, and functional status at one year. Results: Median follow-up was 3.1 years. Mean HbA1c at one year was 6.6% in the intensive group and 7.7% in the standard group. Recurrent stroke occurred in 9.8% and 10.4% respectively (hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.24). Severe hypoglycaemia was more frequent with intensive control (4.1% vs 1.2%). All-cause mortality did not differ. Functional status results are reported in the supplementary appendix. Conclusions: Intensive glucose control did not reduce recurrent stroke and increased severe hypoglycaemia. Trial registration: fictional registry TR-61209.
record.methods_excerpt: Outcome adjudication. A committee of three stroke neurologists, unaware of treatment allocation, adjudicated all suspected strokes using brain imaging and clinical records. Hypoglycaemia was reported by site investigators and classified as severe if third-party assistance was required. Functional status was assessed by trained nurses at one year using the modified Rankin Scale by structured telephone interview; the nurses were not told the allocation, but participants could have mentioned their treatment during the call.

record.abstract: Aims: To understand why patients discontinue statins and how often this happens. record.title: Lung ultrasound for pneumonia in the emergency department: a diagnostic accuracy study
record.abstract: Methods: We recruited 150 adults with pneumonia confirmed on chest CT from the inpatient wards and 150 healthy volunteers from hospital staff. Emergency physicians with at least two years of ultrasound experience performed lung ultrasound and recorded their interpretation before seeing any imaging results. The reference standard was chest CT for patients; volunteers did not undergo CT and were classified as disease-free. Results: Sensitivity was 96% and specificity 98%. Conclusions: Lung ultrasound is highly accurate for pneumonia in emergency settings.
record.methods_excerpt: Chest CT scans for the patient group had been performed as part of routine care before study enrolment and were reported by the duty radiologist. Ultrasound examinations were performed at the bedside on the wards, typically two to four days after admission, when most patients had started antibiotics. Healthy volunteers were scanned in a staff room during working hours. Ultrasound findings were classified as positive if consolidation or focal B-lines were present.

Title: Transcatheter tricuspid valve repair in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation: 1-year outcomes from a single-centre registry

Abstract: Background: Isolated severe tricuspid regurgitation carries a poor prognosis, and many patients are too high-risk for surgery. record.title: Cost-effectiveness of a community health worker-led hypertension programme: a Markov model analysis
record.abstract: Background: Community health worker (CHW) programmes improve blood pressure control, but their long-term cost-effectiveness is uncertain. Methods: We built a Markov model simulating a cohort of 10,000 adults with hypertension over 20 years, comparing a CHW-led programme with standard clinic care. Effect estimates for blood pressure reduction were taken from a pooled analysis of three published randomised trials, including the COMM-BP trial. Costs came from national price lists and a time-and-motion study of CHWs in two districts. Outcomes were cost per disability-adjusted life year averted and cost per person with controlled blood pressure. Results: The CHW programme was cost-effective under most scenarios. Results were sensitive to CHW salary and programme retention. Conclusions: CHW-led hypertension programmes are likely to be cost-effective.
record.discussion_excerpt: Our model relies on trial effects measured over one to two years and assumes they persist, with gradual waning, over twenty years. None of the three trials collected costs prospectively. A trial-based economic evaluation of COMM-BP is in preparation by a different group.

record.title: Melatonin for sleep onset insomnia in children with autism: a randomised placebo-controlled crossover trial
record.abstract: Methods: 48 children aged 4 to 12 years with autism and sleep onset insomnia received melatonin 3 mg or placebo for four weeks each, in random order. Sleep was measured by actigraphy. Results: Sleep onset latency was shorter on melatonin than on placebo (mean difference 24 minutes). Because a period effect was detected, results from the first treatment period are also reported separately: children receiving melatonin first had shorter sleep onset latency than those receiving placebo first. Conclusions: Melatonin shortened sleep onset latency.
record.methods_excerpt_full_text: Each child received melatonin and placebo in random order, four weeks each. Families were asked to stop study capsules at the end of the first period and start the second bottle the following evening. Actigraphy watches were worn continuously; the first three nights of each period were excluded from analysis to allow for adjustment. The sequence was generated by the hospital pharmacy, which dispensed identical-looking bottles labelled 'Period 1' and 'Period 2'. Parents completed a sleep diary each morning.
record.results_excerpt_full_text: Of 48 children randomised, 45 completed both periods. First-period analysis: melatonin-first children (n=23) versus placebo-first children (n=22). Baseline sleep onset latency was longer in the melatonin-first group. A formal test for carryover was not reported.
record.discussion_excerpt: We chose not to include a washout because families told us during planning that a gap without any capsules would be hard to manage and might lead to dropout. We excluded the first three nights of each period from analysis instead, reasoning that melatonin has a short half-life. We acknowledge that behavioural effects of improved sleep, such as changed bedtime routines, could persist beyond the drug's pharmacological action. The period effect we observed may reflect such carryover, or simply the families' growing familiarity with the actigraphy watches.

record.abstract: Methods: 6,200 patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation were randomised in a double-blind, double-dummy design to ZX-44 (a fictional factor Xa inhibitor) or dose-adjusted warfarin. The primary efficacy outcome was stroke or systemic embolism; the primary safety outcome was major bleeding. Results: Stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 1.5% per year with ZX-44 and 1.7% per year with warfarin (non-inferiority met). Major bleeding occurred in 2.1% and 3.0% per year respectively. Intracranial haemorrhage was less frequent with ZX-44. Gastrointestinal bleeding was 'similar'. Conclusions: ZX-44 was non-inferior to warfarin and caused less major bleeding.
record.registry_outcomes: Registered secondary safety outcomes: major bleeding; clinically relevant non-major bleeding; intracranial haemorrhage; gastrointestinal bleeding; liver injury (ALT more than three times the upper limit).
record.full_text_note: The full text reports major bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage and gastrointestinal bleeding with numbers. Clinically relevant non-major bleeding and liver injury are not reported anywhere in the article or its supplement. No explanation is given.
record.regulatory_summary_excerpt: A regulator's public assessment report (fictional) for ZX-44 notes: 'Hepatic laboratory data from ZEPHYR-AF were reviewed. The committee considered the hepatic safety profile acceptable and recommended routine liver monitoring in the product information.' No numbers are given in the public report.
record.funding: Sponsored by the manufacturer of ZX-44, which designed the trial, held the data and drafted the manuscript with the academic steering committee.
record.author_contact: The review team emailed the corresponding author requesting the missing outcomes. The sponsor replied that the data are 'available through the company's data-sharing portal after approval of a research proposal', which typically takes three to six months.
record.steering_committee_letter: In a later letter to the journal, two academic members of the steering committee wrote that clinically relevant non-major bleeding had been 'analysed and discussed' by the committee and was 'broadly similar between groups', and that liver enzyme elevations were 'uncommon and balanced'. They said the omission from the paper reflected 'space constraints' and that the sponsor had agreed to post the full safety tables on the registry, which had not happened at the time of the review's search.

record.title: EPA-enriched omega-3 as adjunctive therapy in major depression: the MOOD-3 randomised placebo-controlled trial
record.abstract: Background: Omega-3 fatty acids have anti-inflammatory properties that may be relevant to depression, and several small trials have reported benefits. Methods: In this 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 310 adults with major depressive disorder confirmed by structured clinical interview, already taking a stable antidepressant, were randomised to 2 g daily of EPA-enriched omega-3 or to olive oil capsules. The primary outcome was change in Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) score at 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes were response (50% reduction in MADRS), remission, and the Beck Depression Inventory. Results: 284 participants completed the trial. The mean change in MADRS did not differ significantly between groups (difference -1.2 points, 95% CI -3.1 to 0.7, p=0.21). Response and remission rates were similar. In participants with high baseline inflammatory markers, MADRS improved more with omega-3 (difference -4.0 points, p=0.03). Gastrointestinal complaints were more frequent with omega-3. Conclusions: EPA-enriched omega-3 significantly improves depressive symptoms in patients with inflammation and represents a promising adjunctive treatment for major depression.
record.methods_note_from_full_text: The inflammatory-marker subgroup analysis is described in the statistical analysis section as 'exploratory'. The trial registry entry lists the primary outcome and three secondary outcomes; it does not mention any subgroup analysis. Eleven subgroup analyses are reported in the supplement (age, sex, baseline severity, antidepressant class, body mass index, smoking, inflammatory markers and four others); only the inflammatory-marker subgroup reached nominal significance, and no correction for multiple testing was applied.
record.funding: Funded by a supplement manufacturer that supplied the capsules. The funder reviewed the manuscript before submission.
record.editorial_comment: An accompanying editorial notes that the trial was well conducted and adequately powered for its primary outcome, which was clearly negative. The editorialists caution that the inflammatory subgroup result, one of eleven exploratory analyses with no correction for multiplicity, should be treated as a hypothesis for a new trial rather than as evidence of benefit, and they question why the abstract's conclusion leads with it. They also note that olive oil is not an inert placebo, although they consider its likely effect on mood small. The journal has invited the authors to respond in a future issue.

Title: Pharmacist-led deprescribing in older adults with polypharmacy: a pragmatic randomised trial in general practice

Abstract: Background: Polypharmacy is common in older adults and linked to falls and hospital admission. Methods: Forty general practices were randomised (1:1) to a pharmacist-led deprescribing service or usual care. All patients aged 75 or older taking ten or more regular medicines were eligible. The primary outcome was the number of regular medicines at 12 months. Outcomes were analysed at the patient level using linear regression adjusted for age, sex and baseline medicine count. Results: 2,840 patients were included (intervention 1,402; control 1,438). At 12 months, patients in intervention practices took fewer regular medicines (difference -1.3, 95% CI -1.5 to -1.1, p<0.001). Hospital admissions did not differ. Conclusions: Pharmacist-led deprescribing reduced medicine burden without increasing admissions.

record.title: Home-based walking programme for fatigue during adjuvant chemotherapy for breast and colorectal cancer: the STEP-CHEMO trial
record.abstract: Background: Fatigue is the most common and distressing symptom during chemotherapy, and exercise may reduce it. Methods: 226 adults starting adjuvant chemotherapy for breast or colorectal cancer at three cancer centres were randomised to a 12-week home-based walking programme or to enhanced usual care. The walking programme set a weekly step target that increased gradually, with a pedometer, weekly phone calls from an exercise physiologist, and a logbook. The enhanced usual care group received a pedometer, the cancer centre's booklet 'Living well during treatment', and a single conversation with a nurse. Fatigue was measured with the FACIT-Fatigue scale at 12 weeks. Results: 201 participants completed follow-up. Fatigue scores were better in the walking group (mean difference 4.1 points, 95% CI 1.6 to 6.6). Quality of life favoured walking; physical function did not differ. One fall occurred in the walking group. Conclusions: A home-based walking programme reduced fatigue during chemotherapy.
record.booklet_contents_from_supplement: The booklet 'Living well during treatment' includes sections on nutrition, sleep, managing nausea, emotional support, and 'staying active', which advises patients to 'keep moving as much as you feel able, for example with short walks'. The booklet is given to every patient starting chemotherapy at the three centres, whether or not they take part in research.
record.nurse_conversation_note: The nurse conversation followed a checklist covering symptom reporting, infection warning signs and whom to call; the full text does not say whether activity was discussed.
record.step_counts_from_full_text: Median daily steps at week 12 were higher in the walking group than in the enhanced usual care group, but the control group's steps also rose from baseline. The authors suggest the pedometer itself may have prompted some control participants to walk more.

record.title: Cognitive behavioural therapy for health anxiety delivered by nurses in general hospitals: the HEAL-CBT randomised trial
record.methods: Design: two-arm, parallel, individually randomised trial in six general hospitals. Participants: adult outpatients attending medical clinics who scored above threshold on the Short Health Anxiety Inventory (SHAI) and met diagnostic criteria for health anxiety on a structured interview. Randomisation: an independent clinical trials unit generated the sequence by computer, stratified by hospital, and allocated participants through a web system after baseline assessment. Interventions: up to ten sessions of CBT adapted for health anxiety, delivered by general nurses trained in a five-day course and supervised fortnightly; control participants received standard care from their medical team. Outcome: the primary outcome was SHAI score at 12 months, self-completed by post. Secondary outcomes included generalised anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9), and health service use from hospital records. Masking: participants and nurses knew the allocation; research assistants who collected secondary outcomes by telephone were masked. Analysis: intention to treat, with multiple imputation for missing primary outcome data under a missing-at-random assumption; sensitivity analyses varied this assumption.
record.results: 444 participants were randomised (222 per arm). Primary outcome data at 12 months were available for 186 (84%) in the CBT arm and 194 (87%) in the control arm. The main reason for missing data was non-return of postal questionnaires; reasons were similar across arms. SHAI scores at 12 months were lower with CBT (adjusted mean difference -2.9, 95% CI -4.1 to -1.7). Sensitivity analyses gave similar results. The number of CBT sessions attended ranged from 0 to 10; 71% attended at least six. Health service use did not differ.
record.registration: Prospectively registered; primary outcome and time point match the registry. A statistical analysis plan was published before the database was locked.
record.other_notes: Four participants in the control arm received CBT privately during follow-up; they were analysed as randomised.
record.discussion: The authors acknowledge that the primary outcome was self-reported by participants who knew whether they had received therapy, and that expectation could have influenced responses. They point out that the secondary anxiety outcome collected by masked assessors showed a similar pattern, and that differences persisted at 12 months, long after the last session, which they consider less compatible with a simple expectation effect. They also note that the control arm did not receive an attention-matched activity, so non-specific effects of contact with a nurse cannot be separated from the specific effects of CBT.

record.title: Intravenous iron before major abdominal surgery in patients with anaemia: the PRE-IRON randomised trial
record.abstract: Background: Preoperative anaemia is associated with transfusion and complications. Methods: 480 adults with iron-deficiency anaemia scheduled for major abdominal surgery were randomised to a single dose of intravenous ferric carboxymaltose or placebo 10 to 42 days before surgery. The primary outcome was the proportion receiving a blood transfusion from randomisation to 30 days after surgery. Results: Transfusion occurred in 28% with iron and 29% with placebo (risk ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.29). Haemoglobin before surgery was higher with iron. The intervention was safe, with no serious adverse events attributable to treatment. Conclusions: Preoperative intravenous iron is a safe and effective way to raise haemoglobin before surgery and should be considered in anaemic patients.
record.results_table_excerpt: Serious adverse events (30 days after surgery): iron 41 (17%), placebo 36 (15%). Deaths: iron 4, placebo 2. Hypophosphataemia (laboratory): iron 19%, placebo 2%. All deaths were judged 'unrelated to study drug' by the site investigators.
record.editorial_note: An accompanying editorial observes that the primary outcome was neutral and that hypophosphataemia after ferric carboxymaltose has been linked in other studies to fatigue and, rarely, osteomalacia. The editorialists add that raising haemoglobin is a surrogate, and that the trial was designed to test transfusion, which it did not reduce. They call for future trials to report patient-centred outcomes such as recovery of function after surgery.
record.authors_reply: In a letter responding to the editorial, the authors state that the haemoglobin rise is 'clinically meaningful in its own right' and that the transfusion result may reflect liberal transfusion practice at some sites. They do not address the hypophosphataemia finding.
record.data_monitoring_note: The trial's independent data monitoring committee reviewed unblinded safety data twice during recruitment and recommended continuing both times. Its final report, published as a supplement, lists the six deaths by cause: two postoperative sepsis, one pulmonary embolism, one myocardial infarction and one anastomotic leak in the iron arm, and one pulmonary embolism and one pneumonia in the placebo arm. The committee did not judge causality; that was left to site investigators. The report notes that phosphate was measured only once, before surgery, so the duration of hypophosphataemia is unknown.

state.text: Protocol outcomes for review SR-2026-1502 (fictional), 'Early mobility programmes in intensive care': O1 ICU-acquired weakness; O2 duration of mechanical ventilation; O3 ICU length of stay; O4 hospital length of stay; O5 physical function at hospital discharge; O6 mortality at 90 days; O7 adverse events during mobilisation; O8 health-related quality of life at 6 months.

Registered outcomes: ICU-acquired weakness (MRC sum score) at ICU discharge; ventilator-free days to day 28; ICU and hospital length of stay; Barthel Index at hospital discharge; mortality at 90 days; safety events during sessions (desaturation, haemodynamic instability, device removal).

MRC sum score at ICU discharge was higher with early mobility. Ventilator-free days did not differ. ICU length of stay was shorter by a median of one day; hospital length of stay did not differ. Barthel Index at discharge favoured early mobility. Mortality at 90 days was similar. Safety events occurred in 0.8% of sessions, none serious.

Quality of life was not registered and not reported. The follow-up paper planned for 6-month outcomes has not appeared. Ventilator-free days is not the same metric as duration of ventilation; check the review's rules on substituting related measures. The trial's supplementary appendix includes a table of daily ventilation status for each participant, from which days of ventilation could in principle be derived, but the table uses codes that are not fully defined in the appendix. I have emailed the trial statistician asking for the code definitions and for days of mechanical ventilation by arm; no reply yet. I also noted that eleven participants were transferred to other ICUs and their ventilation status after transfer is recorded as 'unknown'.

Related measures may be substituted for a protocol outcome only if they are listed in the outcome's 'acceptable measures' table. Acceptable measures for O2: days of mechanical ventilation; time to successful extubation. Ventilator-free days is not listed because it combines death and ventilation. Where an acceptable measure can be derived from individual participant data supplied by the authors, it may be used, with a note in the characteristics of included studies table.

The trial's chief investigator replied to the review team's general enquiry on behalf of the statistician, who is on leave. She said the daily status codes distinguish invasive ventilation, non-invasive ventilation, high-flow oxygen and no support, and that the team would be happy to provide days of invasive mechanical ventilation by arm once the statistician returns next month. She added that the eleven transferred patients could be treated as censored at transfer, and that the team had not planned any quality-of-life follow-up because of funding limits; the 'follow-up paper' mentioned in the discussion concerns 6-month functional outcomes only.

record.title: Five versus ten days of amoxicillin for community-acquired pneumonia in children: the SHORT-CAP non-inferiority randomised trial
record.abstract: Background: Shorter antibiotic courses could reduce side effects and resistance. Methods: Children aged 1 to 10 years with community-acquired pneumonia treated in the community were randomised to 5 or 10 days of amoxicillin, with placebo for days 6 to 10 in the short-course group. The primary outcome was clinical cure at day 28. The non-inferiority margin was 8 percentage points. Results: 620 children were randomised. Clinical cure was 88.1% with 5 days and 89.4% with 10 days (difference -1.3 percentage points, 95% CI -6.0 to 3.4). Diarrhoea was less frequent with the short course. Conclusions: Five days of amoxicillin was non-inferior to ten days.
record.methods_excerpt: The margin of 8 percentage points was chosen after a survey of paediatricians, who were asked what increase in treatment failure they would accept in exchange for a shorter course. The margin was stated in the registered protocol before recruitment began. The per-protocol analysis gave similar results.
record.editorial_comment: An accompanying commentary argued that 8 points is generous for a condition where treatment failure can mean hospital admission, and that a margin of 5 points would have been more defensible. The commentators nonetheless agreed that the trial was well conducted and that its findings support shorter courses for children managed in the community.
record.parent_panel_note: The trial's parent advisory panel, consulted during design, was asked about the margin. Parents said they would accept a small increase in the chance of needing a second course of antibiotics in exchange for fewer doses and less diarrhoea, but several said they would not accept any increase in the chance of hospital admission. The investigators recorded this view in the protocol but kept a single margin for clinical cure, noting that hospital admission was too rare to power separately. Admission rates were reported as a secondary safety outcome and were low in both groups.

review_protocol.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for delirium prevention in older hospitalised adults (fictional protocol)

eligibility.population: Adults aged 65 or older admitted to hospital (medical or surgical wards, excluding intensive care).
eligibility.intervention: Multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions targeting at least three delirium risk factors (for example orientation, sleep, hydration, mobility, sensory aids).
eligibility.outcome: Incident delirium assessed with a validated instrument.
eligibility.design: RCTs, including cluster RCTs with at least two clusters per arm. Non-randomised studies are excluded.

special_rules: S1: Studies that include some ICU patients are eligible if ICU patients are fewer than a fifth of participants or results for non-ICU patients are reported separately.

record.title: A volunteer-delivered delirium prevention programme for older surgical patients: a cluster randomised trial
record.abstract: Background: Delirium after surgery is common and costly. Methods: Eight surgical wards in four hospitals were randomised (four to the programme, four to usual care). Patients aged 70 and over admitted for elective or emergency surgery were eligible. Trained volunteers delivered a daily programme of orientation, cognitive activities, help with meals and fluids, and early walking. Patients transferred to the surgical intensive care unit after surgery continued in the study; 9% of participants spent time in intensive care. Delirium was assessed daily by research nurses using the Confusion Assessment Method, and additionally identified by chart review for days when nurses were unavailable. Results: 1,212 patients were included. Incident delirium occurred in 11.2% on programme wards and 16.8% on usual care wards (odds ratio adjusted for clustering 0.62, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.86). Conclusions: A volunteer-delivered programme reduced postoperative delirium.
record.methods_note_from_full_text: Chart review was used for 6% of patient-days, mainly at weekends. A sensitivity analysis restricted to CAM-assessed days gave a similar result.
record.trial_steering_note: The trial steering committee's report, published with the paper, says that volunteers were recruited through the hospitals' existing volunteer services, trained for two days, and supervised by a ward nurse on each programme ward. Volunteers did not visit patients while they were in intensive care; the programme resumed when patients returned to the ward. The committee noted that research nurses assessing delirium were not told which wards had the programme, but that the presence of volunteers on programme wards would often have been obvious to them. A sensitivity analysis using only chart-review assessments made by staff unaware of the study was not possible because of the small number of such days.
